newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Georgia-Russian ties sour over military bases.
newsitem.headline: Georgia-Russian ties sour over military bases.

text.p: Threats by Georgia to close Russian military bases in the small Caucasus state have put it on a collision course with its former colonial master after three years of improving ties.
Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze said this week that Moscow had been unable to accept the idea that it had lost the mountainous state when the Soviet Union fell apart in 1991.
Russia hit back on Thursday by saying relations could deteriorate over an "anti-Russian campaign" in Georgia.

"Russia is basing its relations with Georgia on trust and mutually profitable ties and if this anti-Russian campaign doesn't stop, it means our relations will be allowed to drift in a negative direction," the Russian foreign ministry said.
The dispute centres on three military bases which Tbilisi has allowed Russia to keep in Georgia.

Shevardnadze, who played a key role in ending the Cold War as Soviet foreign minister, said recently that Moscow should not be able to keep the bases unless it does more to help bring Georgian separatist regions to heel.
"Russia should know that if the territorial integrity of Georgia is not restored, it will not get a single military base in our country," he said.

Stepping up his criticism on Monday, he said: "In Russia they just haven't come to terms with the fact that Georgian-Russian relations are ties between two equal states, and not between a centre and its provinces."
The most sensitive issue is the breakaway Black Sea coastal region of Abkhazia, which Georgia lost to separatist Abkhaz fighters in 1993. The year-long war killed 10,000 people.
Shevardnadze accused Russia of masterminding the defeat in Abkhazia, a former beach playground of the Soviet communist elite, by aiding the rebels with arms and training.

Georgia at the time was not a CIS member and had poor relations with Moscow. Shevardnadze said taking away Abkhazia was a way for Russia to exert leverage over Georgia and make it toe Moscow's foreign policy line.

After Abkhazia fell, Shevardnadze grudgingly signed up Georgia to the Commonwealth of Independent States formed on the ashes of the Soviet Union and let Moscow keep the three military bases on his territory -- something he had earlier resisted.
Shevardnadze now wants 2,500 Russian peacekeepers stationed between Abkhazia and Georgia to take a more active role in helping some 200,000 ethnic Georgian refugees return home.
He wants Moscow to put pressure on the separatist leadership of Vladislav Ardzinba to drop its independence drive.
"The keys to resolving the conflict are in the hands of Russia," he said on Monday.
Many Georgian politicians say their country should leave the CIS and the peacekeepers should go.
They say Russia has failed to hand over former security minister Igor Giorgadze to face Georgian justice, wanted for allegedly organising a bomb attack on Shevardnadze in 1995.
